   10 car brands in S’pore register fewer than 1 car a month; 4 dominate Jan-Sept sales

 Set as preferred source Listen Summarise BYD, Toyota, Tesla and Mercedes-Benz led Singapore’s Jan-Sept 2026 car sales, making up 52.8% of 40,986 new registrations, LTA data showed.
 Ten of 57 brands averaged fewer than one car a month. Some were niche luxury brands, but Peugeot, Ford, KGM and Skyworth were also weak sellers.
 New brands keep entering as high COE prices lift car costs. Dealers rely on aftersales work and wider business interests to stay viable.
 AI generated
 SINGAPORE – In an increasingly crowded car market, 10 of the 57 car brands in Singapore registered fewer than one car per month on average in the first nine months of 2026. At the other end of the spectrum, just four brands accounted for more than half of all new cars on the road.
 Based on car registration data from the Land Transport Authority (LTA) on Oct 26, BYD, Toyota, Tesla and Mercedes-Benz were the strongest performers from January to September. The four brands accounted for 52.8%, or 21,643, of the 40,986 new car registrations.
 The remaining 47.2% was split among 53 other brands with official agents in Singapore.
 While the bottom 10 brands include ultra-luxury and niche sports cars, such as Aston Martin and Lamborghini, which are not expected to sell in large numbers, four are mass-market brands.
 These are French brand Peugeot, American carmaker Ford and Korean brand KGM – which each registered three cars in the first nine months of 2026 – and Chinese electric car brand Skyworth, which registered six units.
 Some brands recorded no new car registrations in recent years. Renault and Mitsubishi did not register any new cars from 2024 to September 2026. Chinese brand Seres, which entered Singapore in 2024, registered eight cars in 2025 but none so far in 2026.
 This comes amid an influx of new car brands, many of them from Chinese carmakers. In 2024, 49 car brands with official representation registered cars in Singapore. This rose to 57 brands in 2025.
 In 2025, 10 c ar brands, including five mass-market ones, registered fewer than 12 cars each. In 2024, seven brands recorded fewer than 12 registrations each, including three mass-market brands.
 A spokesperson for Wearnes Automotive, which represents Renault, said the company is waiting for the carmaker to provide models for the Singapore market. For now, the multi-franchise dealership sells Renault’s commercial vehicles while continuing to support Renault car owners with repairs and maintenance.
 Industry watchers noted that brands with low sales volumes are represented by larger companies with diverse interests or multi-franchise dealerships.
 Seres, for example, is distributed by Hong Seh Group, an 80-year-old local business active in the commercial vehicle sector. It represents brands such as Riddara and Farizon – both sibling brands under Chinese automotive group Geely – and DFSK, another Chinese commercial vehicle brand.
 KGM, previously known as Ssangyong, is distributed by Motorway Group, whose businesses span vehicle distribution, financing, retail and leasing. One of its subsidiaries, Motor-East, is an authorised dealer of BYD. It also owns Lion City Rental, a large car rental and private-hire vehicle leasing company.
 Skyworth is distributed by Think One Group, an automotive group known for its commercial vehicle business, including the distribution of Yutong buses.
 Peugeot, meanwhile, was taken over by multi-franchise motor dealer Cycle & Carriage in 2025, bringing it into the same showroom as Citroen from France and Leapmotor from China.
 All three brands are from the Stellantis automotive group. Peugeot’s range of electric vans is among the stronger performers in the commercial vehicle segment.
 Having other business interests helps dealers spread the costs of representing brands with low sales volumes, said automotive consultant Say Kwee Neng, who headed various car distributorships in Singapore and Taiwan before setting up his own consultancy here.
 He said for most brand dealerships, a healthy after-sales operation – including vehicle servicing, repair and parts – can generate enough revenue to make a dealership’s business viable.
 Established brands have an edge, he added, because there is a larger pool of their cars on the road, translating into business for the after-sales business.
 LTA’s records show that brands such as Renault and Peugeot each had more than 3,000 cars on Singapore’s roads at the end of 2025, while Mitsubishi had more than 16,000.

 Despite low registration numbers for some existing brands, industry sources said as many as six new brands are expected to enter Singapore in the coming months. This comes as car prices are elevated on the back of high certificate of entitlement (COE) premiums.
 At the most recent tender on Oct 21, Category A COE, which is needed to register smaller, less powerful cars and electric vehicles, was priced at $132,004.
 A mass-market car such as the Toyota Corolla Altis costs $230,000 with COE before applicable discounts, higher than the $193,888 in October 2025.
 Lee Nian Tjoe is senior transport correspondent at The Straits Times, where he also oversees the Motoring section.
